summary: Points out a race condition in the Initial Connection Protocol of RFC 123. The problem is that the server tries to open a second connection before the first is closed. Different Network Control Programs handle duplicate requests differently. It was replaced by RFC 165.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people try to hang up and call back at once, and their timing clashes. This note finds that clash in the startup routine.

questions: what is the race condition in the icp
why does the initial connection protocol fail
subtitle: A timing flaw in the connection setup process

tldr.problem: The Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) defined in RFC 123 has a race condition: the server tries to open a second connection before the first is completely closed, causing sockets to conflict.
tldr.mechanism: The race occurs because both the server and user independently decide when to close their connections and open new ones. If these actions overlap, socket numbers collide and operations fail.
tldr.outcome: RFC 143 proposes removing one side's close operation and having that side wait for the other to close first, eliminating the race. It was later replaced by RFC 165 with a more complete solution.

today: RFC 143 was replaced by RFC 165, which provided a more complete specification. The race condition problem it identified highlighted the need for careful ordering of connection management operations.

sections.title: The Race Condition Problem
sections.content: RFC 123 proposed an Initial Connection Procedure (ICP) for establishing connections between computers. However, RFC 143 identifies a timing problem: when the server tries to initiate a second connection while the user's first connection is not yet closed, the ICP can fail. Both the server and user Network Control Programs (NCPs) may attempt to use the same socket numbers at nearly the same moment, causing conflicts.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers try to set up a connection, they sometimes get confused about which sockets to use because they are not waiting for each other.

sections.title: The Sequence of Events
sections.content: The authors provide a detailed sequence of 20 steps showing when actions must occur. The problem manifests when step 16 (the server opening a new socket) happens before step 12 (the user closing its socket). When this occurs, the user's NCP finds its socket already in use from step 16 and may return an error, causing the server to incorrectly assume the user is finished.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tries to open a new connection before the user is done closing the old one. The user gets confused and thinks the conversation is over.

sections.title: The Proposed Solution
sections.content: RFC 143 proposes eliminating the user's explicit close operation and having the user wait for a close signal from the server before opening new connections. This ensures that sockets remain unavailable until the server explicitly releases them. The server's close operation takes precedence, allowing it to reuse sockets for serving the next user more quickly, while the user NCP simply acknowledges the server's close signal before proceeding.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of both sides closing when they want, let the server close first. The user waits and listens, only then opening new connections.

references.text: Guzman, A., "A proposed experiment with message switching protocol", RFC 123, April 1971.
